summary:
Consensual sexual conduct between adults was decriminalised on 16 May 1991 under the Sexual Offences and Domestic Violence Act, and no source records a prosecution risk for a visitor on that basis. The criminal law retains an unequal age of consent: 16 years for opposite-sex acts and 18 years for same-sex acts, so a trans visitor in a relationship that local law reads as same-sex falls under the higher threshold.

Gender identity appears in no anti-discrimination or anti-harassment statute in the Bahamas. Discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, education, housing, healthcare, banking and public businesses is not illegal, and the same gap applies to sexual orientation. The Constitution's prohibition on discrimination covers neither characteristic. The 2006 Constitutional Reform Commission did not regard sexual orientation as deserving protection, and efforts to include it in a proposed Constitution were blocked by members citing religious opposition.

There are no national hate-crime laws to prevent or punish violence directed at LGBT people. A 2001 Employment Bill clause banning sexual-orientation workplace discrimination was removed shortly after passage. The Data Protection (Privacy of Personal Information) Act 2003 lists "sexual life" as sensitive personal data, which is the narrowest statutory protection recorded.

Marriage and partnership recognition is closed: the Marriage Act defines marriage as between a man and a woman, same-sex households are denied the rights given to opposite-sex married couples, and maritime marriage law states a marriage is void if between male-male or female-female. In 2011 former Minister of State Zhivargo Laing stated a marriage is void if between persons of the same sex, calling this a community standard. The 2016 referendum bills were not inclusive of transgender or intersex people, and marriage eligibility was framed as between a man and a woman with male and female determined at birth.

Official hostility toward trans people is documented at the political level. Government member Leslie Miller publicly called for the "Exile of Transgender out of the Bahamas," urging financial contributions to relocate transgender people to a private island so "they stay out of the way" and pledging $1,000 toward it. Former Prime Minister Perry Christie stated in 2013 he did not believe in same-sex marriage and in 2016 said a referendum would not legalise it, defining marriage as between male and female determined at birth.

Bahamas Transgender, Intersex United launched the 'Bahamian Trans Lives Matter' campaign on 27 April 2016, stressing that no laws protect transgender and intersex Bahamians; member Torri Culmer advocates against job termination for trans and intersex workers. This is organised advocacy in the face of a documented absence of trans-specific legal protection.

Violent targeting of a gay visitor during a major tourist event is documented: on 8 May 2017 Adrian Brown, 24, Jamaica-born and US-resident, was treated at Doctors Hospital for a head laceration after being targeted and beaten because he is gay at Bahamas Junkanoo Carnival, and he wants charges laid. There are no national hate-crime laws under which such an attack would be charged as a bias crime.

Juries have acquitted or leniently sentenced killers invoking gay-panic defences, including a 2009 acquittal for the murder of a homosexual HIV-positive man and a 10 June 2010 case in which the Court of Appeal president stated "One is entitled to use whatever force is necessary to prevent one's self-being the victim of a homosexual act." Nine murders of gay men between 2001 and 2015 remain unsolved, including an accused in the 2007 Harl Taylor slaying found not guilty. The most recent documented case in this record is from 2017; no later instance is documented.

Social conditions constrain visibility. Many Bahamians belong to conservative Christian denominations treating homosexuality and cross-dressing as decadence, and politicians have been leery of publicly supporting LGBT-rights legislation. Surveys record 85.5% strongly disapproving of same-sex marriage in 2015 with 10.6% approving, and over 84% strongly disapproving of a gay or lesbian politician in 2013 with 12% positive; these figures measure attitudes toward sexual orientation, not gender identity specifically. Due to lack of confidence in the judicial system, legal inequalities and homophobia, many LGBT people keep sexual orientation or gender identity private, and LGBT groups are often pressured to keep social events hidden. No exclusively gay bars or clubs exist; the Nassau scene is underground.

Police raided a gay party in downtown Nassau on 6 October 2007 with no arrests, and the Ministry of Tourism later apologised. Groups of LGBT tourists have been protested, including church group opposition to Rosie O'Donnell's 2004 cruise and a 1998 protest against a lesbian cruise; in September 2007 the Bahamas Christian Council formed an anti-gay committee over a request to a local cable company to carry the LGBTQ channel Logo. The Plays and Films Control Board banned Brokeback Mountain in March 2006 and attempted to block a public-square screening of Children of God on 24 June 2011, though the government overruled it.

In May 1998 National Security Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Frank Watson announced the military, prison service and police do not discriminate on the basis of sexual orientation, and LGBT citizens face no prohibition on serving in those forces. The Communications Act 2009 empowers URCA to issue codes of practice against content likely to incite hatred or vilify persons on the basis of sexual preference. In 2005 an 18-year-old beauty queen had her crown stripped after confirming she was a lesbian. In 2016 the Canadian government issued travel advice warning gay couples about the risk of homophobia in the Bahamas. No HIV-specific or trans-specific care provisions are recorded.
tangentialFactors:
The 2016 Canadian travel advice warning to gay couples about homophobia in the Bahamas is a foreign-government risk signal, though it addresses sexual orientation rather than gender identity.

The 2009 acquittal and the 10 June 2010 Court of Appeal remark legitimising force against a homosexual act indicate judicial tolerance of gay-panic reasoning, which bears on how violence against gender-nonconforming people would be treated in court.

The 2007 Nassau party raid produced a Ministry of Tourism apology, showing that tourist-facing authorities have previously distanced themselves from anti-LGBT policing, but no trans-specific incident of this kind is documented.

Attitude surveys from 2013 and 2015 measure disapproval of same-sex marriage and of gay or lesbian politicians, not attitudes toward trans people; no comparable trans-specific survey figure appears in the inventory.
